dcaBacktest.question: What is a DCA backtest?
dcaBacktest.answer: A DCA backtest simulates investing a fixed amount every month into an ETF or stock over a historical period, then estimates shares accumulated, ending value, profit, and total return.

compoundInterest.question: What is compound interest?
compoundInterest.answer: Compound interest is growth on both your original investment and prior gains. Over long periods, reinvested returns can become a major part of portfolio growth.

monthlyGrowth.question: How does monthly investing grow over time?
monthlyGrowth.answer: Monthly investing can grow through consistent contributions and market returns. The DCA backtest uses historical monthly prices where available, while the compound calculator projects future growth from your assumptions.

vooCspx.question: Can I backtest VOO or CSPX?
vooCspx.answer: Yes. You can select supported markets and assets such as VOO and CSPX. When historical CSV data is available, the backtest uses it; otherwise the calculator clearly falls back to sample data.

financialAdvice.question: Is this calculator investment advice?
financialAdvice.answer: No. Past performance does not guarantee future results. DCA Backtest is for educational purposes only and is not financial advice.

free.question: Is this calculator free?
free.answer: Yes. The DCA backtest calculator and compound interest calculator are currently free to use.

etfs.question: Can I use this for ETFs?
etfs.answer: Yes. The tool is designed for ETF monthly investing examples such as VOO, SPY, QQQ, CSPX, and other supported ETFs where data is available.

sampleData.question: Why do some assets use sample data?
sampleData.answer: Some global instruments do not have imported historical CSV files yet. When that happens, the calculator clearly marks the result as sample data instead of presenting it as real historical data.

marketDataUpdates.question: How often is market data updated?
marketDataUpdates.answer: Market data is updated manually for now when new CSV files are imported. The site does not use a real-time market data API yet.

seoContent.title: Learn how DCA backtesting and compound growth work
seoContent.intro: Use this DCA calculator, compound interest calculator, ETF investment calculator, and monthly investment calculator to explore long-term investing scenarios for VOO, CSPX, ETFs, and stocks.

dca.title: What is dollar-cost averaging?
dca.body: Dollar-cost averaging means investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule. A DCA backtest calculator helps you compare how that habit may have performed across different market years.

compound.title: What is compound interest?
compound.body: Compound interest is the effect of earning returns on both your invested capital and previous gains. A compound interest calculator can show how small monthly contributions may grow over long periods.

dcaVsLumpSum.title: DCA vs lump sum investing
dcaVsLumpSum.body: DCA spreads purchases over time, while lump sum investing commits capital at once. This tool focuses on monthly investing so you can compare steady contribution behavior against historical market prices.

howToUse.title: How to use this DCA backtest calculator
howToUse.body: Choose a market, asset type, ETF or stock, monthly investment amount, start year, and end year. The calculator estimates total invested, shares accumulated, ending value, profit, and return.

etfExample.title: ETF monthly investing example
etfExample.body: For example, a VOO DCA calculator or CSPX DCA calculator can model how regular ETF investing may have grown using historical monthly prices where data is available.

supportedAssets.title: Supported assets and markets
supportedAssets.body: The calculator supports selected ETFs and stocks across the United States, Ireland UCITS, Taiwan, Malaysia, Singapore, Japan, and Hong Kong. Assets without imported market data clearly use sample data.

disclaimer.title: Important disclaimer
disclaimer.body: This tool is for education only and is not financial advice. Past performance does not guarantee future results, and real returns can differ because of fees, taxes, dividends, execution prices, and currency conversion.
